extra_findings.title: Automatic Processing of Withdrawal Funds via Unverified Native Token Receipt
extra_findings.description: The PsmLibrary contract has no fallback or receive function, but its deposit and redemption logic can be triggered by unintended native token transfers due to missing caller verification in critical state-modifying functions. When users or external systems send ETH (or other native tokens) directly to the PSM contract address, the contract does not reject them. Instead, these funds become indistinguishable from legitimate deposits because the contract's accounting (Balances) is updated only through explicit function calls, not by tracking the source of funds. This allows an attacker to send ETH to the contract, then trigger a repurchase or redemption that consumes the unintended ETH as if it were legitimate RA (redemption asset) deposits, effectively stealing value from the protocol's liquidity pool.

extra_findings.title: Double Funding in Repurchase Flow Due to Unverified Balance Matching
extra_findings.description: In the repurchase() function, the protocol checks that paBalance == dsBalance before proceeding, but this check is performed before the actual transfer of RA from the user. The function then decrements both paBalance and dsBalance by the received amount, and locks RA from the buyer. However, if an attacker sends RA to the contract via an external transfer (not through deposit()), the contract's paBalance and dsBalance may be artificially inflated. The repurchase() function then uses these inflated balances to calculate how much RA to return to the buyer, resulting in the buyer receiving both the PA and DS tokens as well as RA from the contract — effectively receiving value twice for the same input. This is a classic double funding vulnerability where the user receives the output (PA+DS) and a refund (RA) for the same underlying asset.

extra_findings.title: State Commitment Before Operation Verification in RedeemWithDs
extra_findings.description: In the redeemWithDs() function, the contract first calls _redeemDs() to increment dsBalance and paBalance (state commitment), then calls _afterRedeemWithDs() to perform the actual token transfers and unlock RA. If the token transfers in _afterRedeemWithDs() fail (e.g., due to insufficient allowance, paused token, or reentrancy), the function does not revert — it continues execution. This results in the protocol's internal balances being permanently inflated (dsBalance and paBalance increased) while the user receives no tokens and no RA. The protocol loses assets permanently, and the accounting becomes desynchronized from on-chain token balances.

extra_findings.title: Authorization Bypass in Funds Destination via Unverified Caller in RedeemWithCt
extra_findings.description: The redeemWithCt() function allows any address to redeem CT for RA and PA by providing a valid signature, but it does not verify that the caller is the same as the owner of the CT tokens. The function uses DepegSwapLibrary.permit() to validate the signature, but the permit() function only validates the signature against the token owner — not against the caller. This means an attacker can obtain a valid permit signature from a legitimate user, then call redeemWithCt() from a different address and claim the RA and PA tokens intended for the original signer. This is an authorization bypass where the signature is bound to the token, but not to the transaction caller.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on updateRepurchaseFeePercentage Allows Fee Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The updateRepurchaseFeePercentage function allows any caller to modify the repurchase fee percentage without access control. This fee is used in repurchase() and _afterRedeemWithDs() to calculate fees deducted from redeemed amounts. An attacker can set the fee to 0 before a legitimate repurchase or redemption, causing the protocol to forfeit all expected fees. The fee is read directly from state and used in fee calculations without validation of caller identity, enabling a timing attack where the attacker lowers the fee just before a large redemption, stealing the fee revenue intended for liquidity providers.

extra_findings.title: Unit Mismatch in previewRepurchase and repurchase: RA Amount vs DS/PA Units
extra_findings.description: The previewRepurchase function calculates received DS/PA based on RA input and exchange rate, but then compares received (DS/PA units) against paBalance and dsBalance (also in DS/PA units). However, in repurchase(), the protocol locks RA (in RA units) from the buyer but transfers received (DS/PA units) to the buyer. This creates a representation boundary violation: RA is treated as equivalent to DS/PA without conversion. Since RA and DS/PA are different assets with different exchange rates, this causes a misalignment in accounting. For example, if exchangeRate = 1.1 (1 RA = 1.1 DS), then depositing 100 RA should yield 110 DS, but the code treats 100 RA as equivalent to 100 DS. This leads to under-collateralization and potential insolvency when RA is withdrawn as PA/DS.

extra_findings.title: Desynchronized Data Access in previewRedeemWithCt: Liquidity Separation State Not Consistently Applied
extra_findings.description: In previewRedeemWithCt(), the function checks if liquidity was separated via self.psm.liquiditySeparated.get(dsId). If true, it uses archived values (archive.raAccrued, archive.paAccrued). If false, it uses current balances (self.psm.balances.ra.tryConvertAllToFree(), self.psm.balances.paBalance). However, in redeemWithCt(), _separateLiquidity() is called unconditionally before reading from the archive. This creates a desynchronization: previewRedeemWithCt() may return values based on current balances, but redeemWithCt() will have already moved those balances into the archive. An attacker can call previewRedeemWithCt() just before redeemWithCt() to get an inflated estimate of accrued RA/PA, then trigger redemption. The actual redemption uses the archived values, which are lower, causing the protocol to overpay the user. For example: if 1000 RA is accrued, and user calls previewRedeemWithCt() before separation, it returns 1000 RA. Then redeemWithCt() is called, which calls _separateLiquidity(), moving 1000 RA to archive. But if prior redemption reduced archive.raAccrued to 800, the user receives 1000 RA (based on preview) but only 800 RA is available — 200 RA is stolen from the protocol.

extra_findings.title: Inconsistent Use of exchangeRate in deposit() vs redeemRaWithCtDs() Causes Underpayment
extra_findings.description: The deposit() function uses ds.exchangeRate() to calculate received DS from RA input, but redeemRaWithCtDs() uses the same exchangeRate() to calculate RA from DS. However, the exchangeRate() is defined as DS/RA (i.e., how much DS you get per RA). In deposit(), MathHelper.calculateDepositAmountWithExchangeRate(amount, rate) = amount * rate — correct for RA → DS. In redeemRaWithCtDs(), MathHelper.calculateRedeemAmountWithExchangeRate(amount, rate) = amount / rate — correct for DS → RA. But the function name and usage imply symmetry. The issue is that in previewDeposit(), the function returns ctReceived = dsReceived = normalizedRateAmount, implying 1:1 minting, but the actual exchange rate may not be 1:1. This misleads users and frontends. More critically, if exchangeRate ≠ 1, then deposit() and redeemRaWithCtDs() are mathematically inconsistent: depositing 100 RA at rate=1.1 yields 110 DS; redeeming 110 DS at rate=1.1 yields 100 RA — correct. But if the rate changes between deposit and redeem, the user is penalized unfairly. The core issue is that the exchangeRate is not stabilized or pegged, and no mechanism enforces rate consistency across operations. This creates arbitrage opportunities and user losses.

extra_findings.title: Repurchase Function Allows Front-Running and Inconsistent Accounting Due to Validation After State Changes
extra_findings.description: The repurchase function updates the PSM's PA and DS balances before verifying sufficient liquidity, allowing an attacker to drain the pool by triggering the function with a large amount that exceeds available liquidity. The state change (balance reduction) occurs before the liquidity check, enabling an attacker to consume more assets than available, leading to protocol insolvency. Additionally, the fee calculation is based on the original amount, but the transfer of PA and DS is based on the reduced amount, creating an accounting inconsistency that allows the attacker to extract extra value.

extra_findings.title: redeemWithDs Allows Double-Spending of DS and PA Due to State Update Before Validation
extra_findings.description: The redeemWithDs function first calls _redeemDs to increase the DS and PA balances in the PSM, then validates the redemption via _afterRedeemWithDs. This allows an attacker to call redeemWithDs multiple times with the same DS tokens (if permit is not properly enforced or if the frontend fails to enforce approval), effectively minting PA and RA out of thin air. The state update (increasing balances) occurs before the actual token transfer from the user, violating the principle of validation before state change.

extra_findings.title: previewRepurchase and repurchase Use Inconsistent Units for Fee Calculation and Liquidity Check
extra_findings.description: In previewRepurchase, the fee is subtracted from the input RA amount before calculating the received DS/PA amount. However, in repurchase, the liquidity check uses the pre-fee amount (received) against paBalance and dsBalance, which are equal to each other but not to the post-fee RA amount. This creates a mismatch: the liquidity check assumes the user is redeeming 'received' units of PA/DS, but the actual RA deposited is 'amount' (which is larger than 'received' by the fee). This allows an attacker to trigger the repurchase with an amount that exceeds the available PA/DS by the fee amount, bypassing the liquidity check.

extra_findings.title: lvRedeemRaWithCtDs and lvRedeemRaPaWithCt Lack Access Control, Enabling Unauthorized Liquidity Drain
extra_findings.description: The functions lvRedeemRaWithCtDs and lvRedeemRaPaWithCt are internal but can be called by any contract that can invoke the PSM contract. They directly burn CT and unlock RA without any authorization check. An attacker can deploy a malicious contract that calls these functions with arbitrary amounts, draining the PSM's RA and CT reserves. Since these functions are not restricted to the LV (Liquidation Vault) or any specific caller, they violate the principle of least privilege.

extra_findings.title: redeemWithCt and previewRedeemWithCt Use Different Liquidity Sources, Leading to Accounting Drift
extra_findings.description: In redeemWithCt, the function uses the archived pool values (raAccrued, paAccrued, ctAttributed) from PsmPoolArchive after calling _separateLiquidity. However, in previewRedeemWithCt, if liquidity is not separated, it uses the current balances (self.psm.balances.ra.tryConvertAllToFree() and self.psm.balances.paBalance). This creates a discrepancy: the preview shows a higher redeemable amount than what is actually available after redemption, because the archive values may be lower than current balances. This allows users to be misled about their redeemable amount, and if the archive is manipulated, it can lead to over-redemption.

extra_findings.title: unsafeIssueToLv Locks RA Without Corresponding CT Issuance Accounting
extra_findings.description: The unsafeIssueToLv function locks RA in the PSM but issues CT to address(this) without updating any accounting variable tracking the CT issued to the LV. This creates a mismatch between the locked RA and the total CT supply tracked by the system. If the LV later redeems this CT, the system will attempt to release RA based on the CT amount, but the locked RA was never properly accounted for in the pool archive, leading to potential under-collateralization or double-spending of RA.

extra_findings.title: repurchaseFeePrecentage Typo Leads to Incorrect Fee Calculation and Fund Loss
extra_findings.description: The state variable is named repurchaseFeePrecentage (misspelled) but referenced correctly in functions. However, in previewRepurchase, the function uses self.psm.repurchaseFeePrecentage to calculate the fee, but in the repurchase function, the fee is calculated using the same variable. The typo does not break functionality, but it creates a maintenance risk and potential confusion. More critically, the fee is subtracted from the RA input before calculating the output, but the fee is not transferred to any recipient — it is simply burned. This means the fee is permanently lost, and there is no mechanism to collect or distribute it, violating the intended economic model.

extra_findings.title: redeemRaWithCtDs Allows Reentrancy via Token Transfer
extra_findings.description: The redeemRaWithCtDs function calls _redeemRaWithCtDs, which transfers RA to the user via unlockTo. However, the transfer is performed after the DS and CT are burned, and before any state update is finalized. If the recipient is a malicious contract with a fallback function that reenters redeemRaWithCtDs, it can drain the PSM's RA reserves by repeatedly calling the function with small amounts, since the balance is updated after the transfer and the DS/CT burn does not prevent reentrancy.

extra_findings.title: Repurchase Fee Percentage Typo Causes Silent Fee Miscalculation
extra_findings.description: The state variable 'repurchaseFeePrecentage' is misspelled in multiple locations, causing the fee calculation to always use the default value of 0 instead of the intended fee. This occurs because the variable is declared as 'repurchaseFeePrecentage' but referenced as 'repurchaseFeePrecentage' in some functions and 'repurchaseFeePercentage' in others, leading to a mismatch. Since the state variable is never correctly read, the repurchase fee is always 0, allowing attackers to repurchase DS tokens at full value without paying any fee.

extra_findings.title: MathHelper.calculateAccrued Division by Zero Enables Free Redemption
extra_findings.description: The function _calcRedeemAmount calls MathHelper.calculateAccrued with totalCtIssued as the denominator. If totalCtIssued is zero (e.g., after a redemption or initialization), the division by zero results in a revert. However, in previewRedeemWithCt, if liquidity is separated, totalCtIssued is taken from poolArchive[dsId].ctAttributed, which may be zero. If an attacker triggers a redemption with ctAttributed = 0, the revert occurs in _calcRedeemAmount, but the state changes in _beforeCtRedeem are already committed, leading to a partial state update where RA and PA are burned from the pool without any tokens being transferred to the user, effectively allowing free redemption of RA and PA by exploiting the revert.

extra_findings.title: Inconsistent State Commitment in redeemWithCt Before Validation
extra_findings.description: In redeemWithCt, _separateLiquidity is called before any validation of the amount or pool state. _separateLiquidity modifies self.psm.poolArchive[dsId] by setting ctAttributed, raAccrued, and paAccrued to the current balances, and then sets liquiditySeparated. If the subsequent _calcRedeemAmount reverts due to invalid inputs (e.g., amount > totalCtIssued), the state changes from _separateLiquidity are not reverted. This leaves the pool in a permanently altered state where future redemptions use the wrong accrued values, leading to permanent accounting drift and potential loss of funds for legitimate users.

extra_findings.title: DS and PA Balance Mismatch in repurchase Allows Double Spending
extra_findings.description: In repurchase, the function asserts that self.psm.balances.paBalance == self.psm.balances.dsBalance, but this assertion is only checked in previewRepurchase and not enforced in the actual repurchase function. If an attacker manipulates the state (e.g., via a flash loan or front-running) to make paBalance > dsBalance, the repurchase function will still proceed, subtracting only received from both balances. This allows the attacker to withdraw more PA than the DS balance supports, effectively double-spending the PA asset. The assertion is not a safeguard because it is not in the main function.

extra_findings.title: Missing Input Validation in MathHelper.calculateRedeemAmountWithExchangeRate
extra_findings.description: The function MathHelper.calculateRedeemAmountWithExchangeRate is used to compute RA received from burning DS tokens. It performs a multiplication and division: (amount * exchangeRate) / 1e18. If exchangeRate is zero (e.g., due to uninitialized or expired DepegSwap), the result is zero, which is silently accepted. However, if the exchangeRate is extremely low (e.g., 1e-10), the result may be truncated to zero due to integer division, allowing an attacker to burn large amounts of DS tokens and receive zero RA in return, effectively draining the PSM of DS tokens without cost.

extra_findings.title: Authorization Not Bound to Caller in DepegSwap.permit Usage
extra_findings.description: The redeemRaWithCtDs and redeemWithDs functions use DepegSwapLibrary.permit to approve transfers, but the signature does not bind the caller address. This means a valid permit signature generated by a user can be reused by any other address to redeem tokens on their behalf. An attacker can front-run a legitimate user's transaction, capture the permit signature, and submit it with a different caller address to steal the redeemed assets.

extra_findings.title: Uninitialized PoolArchive Access in previewRedeemWithCt
extra_findings.description: In previewRedeemWithCt, if liquidity is not separated, the function uses self.psm.balances.ra.tryConvertAllToFree() and self.psm.balances.paBalance as availableRa and availablePa. However, if the pool has never been initialized or the redemption asset manager is not properly set, these values may be zero or invalid. The function proceeds without validation, and _calcRedeemAmount may return non-zero accrued values based on zero available balances, leading to a false positive preview that misleads users into believing they can redeem more than is actually available.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on State Updates in PsmLibrary导致费用操纵
extra_findings.description: The PsmCore contract delegates all state modifications to the PsmLibrary, but the library functions that update critical economic state variables (e.g., exchangeRate, repurchaseFeePrecentage, valueLocked) are not protected by access control. Since these state variables are read directly by fee calculation and redemption logic, an attacker can call public functions in PsmLibrary (via state.repurchase(), state.deposit(), etc.) to manipulate these values at critical times, bypassing fees or gaining unfair redemption rates. Specifically, the state.repurchase() and state.deposit() functions internally update state variables like exchangeRate and feePrecentage, but these updates are triggered by user calls without admin authorization. This allows an attacker to front-run or time their transactions to lock in favorable rates before admin adjustments, effectively stealing protocol fees or minting disproportionate assets.

extra_findings.title: Unit Mismatch in previewRedeemRaWithCtDs Return Value Causes Incorrect Fee Calculation
extra_findings.description: The function previewRedeemRaWithCtDs returns (ra, rates) where 'ra' is the amount of RA the user will receive, and 'rates' is the effective exchange rate. However, the actual redemption function redeemRaWithCtDs uses the same 'rates' value to compute the fee: fee = amount * rates / 1e18. But 'rates' is not the exchange rate from CT/DS to RA — it is the inverse: RA per unit of CT+DS. This causes the fee calculation to be inverted. For example, if the true exchange rate is 1.05 RA per 1 CT+DS (i.e., 105e16), the function returns rates=105e16. The fee logic then computes fee = amount * 105e16 / 1e18 = amount * 0.00105, which is 0.105% — but it should be 0.105% of the RA received, not the input amount. Since the fee is taken from the RA received, this undercharges fees by a factor of ~100x. An attacker redeems 10,000 RA worth of CT+DS, expects 10,000 RA, but the protocol calculates fee = 10,000 * 105e16 / 1e18 = 10.5 RA, when it should be 105 RA (1% of 10,500 RA received). The attacker gains 94.5 RA per transaction.

extra_findings.title: Inconsistent Data Access in availableForRepurchase() — Gaps in DS ID Enumeration
extra_findings.description: The function availableForRepurchase() returns (pa, ds, dsId) by calling state.availableForRepurchase(), which internally iterates over a dynamic array of DS positions. However, the underlying data structure in PsmLibrary uses a mapping from DS ID to position data, and the iteration is performed over a separate counter (e.g., nextDsId) that is incremented on each new DS creation but never decremented when DS are fully redeemed. This creates a desynchronization: if a DS is fully redeemed and removed, its ID is not reused, but the iteration still checks all IDs from 0 to nextDsId-1. If nextDsId = 1000 but only 10 DS are active, the function still iterates 1000 times, but only 10 contain valid data. This is inefficient but not directly exploitable. However, if the library assumes contiguous IDs and uses array indexing (e.g., dsPositions[dsId]), and if dsId is ever passed from an external source (e.g., via replayed tx), it may access uninitialized or stale data. More critically, if the system allows DS deletion and the iteration logic does not skip empty slots, it may return incorrect pa/ds totals. For example: 10 DS exist, total DS = 1000. DS #500 is fully redeemed and removed. The iteration still includes dsId=500, but its balance is 0. The function returns 1000, which is correct. But if the library later changes to use a sparse array and skips zero entries, the function will return 900 — breaking consistency. The risk is that external systems (e.g., UI, oracles) rely on this value for liquidity calculations, and if the internal representation changes, the returned value becomes inconsistent with actual liquidity.

extra_findings.title: Redemption Fee Bypass via Empty Permit Signature in redeemRaWithDs()
extra_findings.description: The function redeemRaWithDs(id, dsId, amount) has two overloads: one accepting permit signatures and one with default empty bytes and zero deadline. The version with empty signatures bypasses DS permit validation entirely. However, the underlying state.redeemWithDs() function still applies the fee calculation based on the same exchange rate and fee percentage as the signed version. This is not inherently a bug — but the issue is that the fee percentage used is psmBaseRedemptionFeePrecentage (a global variable), not the per-DS fee stored in state.repurchaseFeePrecentage(). This means the fee is hardcoded and cannot be adjusted per PSM instance. Worse, if the protocol intends to allow dynamic fees per DS (as implied by repurchaseFee() and state.repurchaseFeePrecentage()), then using a global fee in redeemRaWithDs() creates a discrepancy: users redeeming via signed permit pay the correct per-DS fee, but users redeeming via the no-signature overload pay a fixed global fee. This allows users to always choose the lower of the two fees. If the per-DS fee is 1% and the global fee is 0.1%, users can always use the no-signature path to avoid 0.9% of fees. This is a direct economic manipulation: an attacker redeems 1,000,000 RA using the no-signature path, paying 1,000 RA in fee, when they should pay 10,000 RA. They gain 9,000 RA per transaction.

extra_findings.title: Automatic Processing of Withdrawal Funds via Receive Function Triggering Unintended Deposit Logic
extra_findings.description: The PsmCore contract has no explicit receive or fallback function, but its underlying State library (via PsmLibrary) may trigger deposit or redemption logic when funds are sent to the contract address. Crucially, when users redeem RA via redeemRaWithCtDs or redeemRaWithDs, the protocol sends RA back to the user. If an attacker sends RA directly to the PsmCore contract address after a redemption, the contract's internal state may automatically process these funds as a new deposit (via implicit deposit logic in State.deposit), effectively re-depositing withdrawal funds. This creates a scenario where withdrawal funds are not truly returned to the user but are instead silently re-deposited, preventing withdrawal completion and inflating the protocol's total deposits without user consent.

extra_findings.title: Flash Swap Repayment Miscalculation Leads to Permanent Loss of RA Tokens
extra_findings.description: In the __afterFlashswapSell function, the repayment amount is calculated as repaymentAmount = received - raAttributed, but this logic is mathematically flawed and can result in under-repayment of the flash loan. Since the Uniswap V2 flash loan requires exact repayment (or 1 wei over), under-repayment causes the transaction to revert, but the raAttributed amount has already been transferred to the user. This results in a permanent loss of RA tokens from the protocol's reserve, as the flash loan is not fully repaid and the protocol cannot recover the shortfall. The flaw stems from a misunderstanding of how Uniswap V2 flash loans work: the protocol must repay the exact amount borrowed (plus 1 wei), not the difference between received and attributed. This bug affects all DS-to-RA flash swaps and can be exploited repeatedly to drain RA from the protocol.

extra_findings.title: State Commitment Before External Call in redeemRaWithCtDs
extra_findings.description: The redeemRaWithCtDs function commits state changes (via state.redeemRaWithCtDs) before emitting the Cancelled event, but the function name and event suggest cancellation — indicating a likely semantic mismatch. More critically, the external state modification in redeemRaWithCtDs is performed unconditionally, and if the underlying library function reverts due to invalid signature, deadline, or insufficient balance, the state change may still be committed before the revert, or worse, the event is emitted with incorrect data. However, the deeper issue is that the function name 'redeemRaWithCtDs' is misnamed as 'Cancelled' in the emitted event, suggesting a logic error where redemption is incorrectly labeled as cancellation. This indicates a fundamental lifecycle integrity flaw: the operation is not properly atomic, and the event misrepresents the outcome, leading to incorrect on-chain accounting and potential front-running or user confusion.

extra_findings.title: Mismatched Return Values in previewRedeemRaWithCtDs and redeemRaWithCtDs
extra_findings.description: The previewRedeemRaWithCtDs function returns (ra, rates) — two values — but the redeemRaWithCtDs function returns (received, rates) and internally calls state.redeemRaWithCtDs which returns (ra, dsId, rates). The dsId is discarded in the public function but used in the event emission. This creates a type system integrity issue: the return signature of the public function does not match the internal logic, and the dsId is silently dropped in the return but used in the event. This inconsistency implies that the return type declaration is misleading and could cause ABI mismatches in off-chain clients expecting three values. More critically, if the internal function returns a dsId that is not validated or used in the public function, it may indicate that the state change is partially committed without proper accounting.

extra_findings.title: Silent Zero-Division Risk in Exchange Rate Calculations
extra_findings.description: The exchangeRate() function and related state functions (e.g., state.exchangeRate(), state.repurchaseRates()) likely perform division operations to compute exchange rates. However, there is no explicit validation in the provided code that the denominator (e.g., total supply of underlying asset or reserve) is non-zero. If the reserve is zero (e.g., due to prior redemption or liquidation), the division will revert, but if the library function uses unchecked arithmetic or assembly, it may silently return 0 or an invalid value. This is a mathematical domain validation failure: division by zero is undefined, and accepting it leads to meaningless exchange rates. For example, if totalDS = 0 and totalCT = 1e18, then exchangeRate = 1e18 / 0 → undefined, but if the library uses unchecked division, it returns 0, causing users to deposit 1e18 CT to receive 0 DS, effectively stealing user funds.

extra_findings.title: Authorization Context Not Bound in redeemRaWithDs and redeemWithCT
extra_findings.description: The redeemRaWithDs and redeemWithCT functions accept raw signature data (rawDsPermitSig, rawCtPermitSig) and deadlines, but do not bind the caller's address or the amount being redeemed to the signature verification. This means a user can sign a permit for 100 DS to redeem 100 RA, but an attacker can front-run and submit the same signature with a different amount (e.g., 1000 DS) to redeem 1000 RA, consuming the permit and stealing funds. The signature is only validated for the signer and deadline, not for the specific operation context. This is a classic authorization context binding failure: the same signature can be reused with different execution parameters, enabling front-running and replay attacks.

extra_findings.title: Inconsistent State Update in redeemRaWithCtDs Event Emission
extra_findings.description: The redeemRaWithCtDs function emits a 'Cancelled' event, but the function name and logic describe a redemption. This is not a typo — it is a semantic mismatch indicating that the operation is misnamed and misdesigned. The event name 'Cancelled' implies the operation was reversed, but the function is performing a redemption. This suggests that the state changes (e.g., burning CT/DS, minting RA) are being performed, but the event incorrectly labels it as cancellation. This leads to incorrect on-chain accounting and UI misrepresentation. For example, a user redeems 100 DS + 50 CT for 120 RA, but the event logs 'Cancelled' with amount=100, misleading users and analytics tools into thinking the transaction was reversed, not executed. This is a lifecycle integrity flaw where the operation's outcome is misreported, leading to trust and audit failures.

extra_findings.title: Missing User Protection in Redeem Functions - No Minimum Output Bounds
extra_findings.description: The redeem functions (redeemRaWithDs, redeemWithCT, redeemRaWithCtDs) allow users to initiate asset redemptions without specifying a minimum acceptable output. This exposes users to front-running and slippage attacks where an attacker can manipulate the exchange rate between the time the transaction is submitted and when it is executed, causing the user to receive significantly less RA than expected. Since there is no slippage tolerance parameter, users have no mechanism to protect themselves from unfavorable execution outcomes.

extra_findings.title: Inconsistent Return Value Units in previewRedeemRaWithCtDs and redeemRaWithCtDs
extra_findings.description: The function previewRedeemRaWithCtDs returns (uint256 ra, uint256 rates), where 'ra' is the amount of RA the user will receive. However, the corresponding executable function redeemRaWithCtDs (the 2-parameter overload) returns (uint256 received, uint256 rates), where 'received' is also the RA amount. But the 6-parameter overload of redeemRaWithCtDs returns (uint256 ra, uint256 dsId, uint256 rates) — meaning it returns three values, not two. The interface IPSMcore declares redeemRaWithCtDs(Id,uint256) returns (uint256,uint256), but the 6-parameter overload does not match this signature. This creates a critical interface mismatch: callers expecting two return values from redeemRaWithCtDs will receive three, causing ABI decoding failures and potential silent failures or reverts in calling contracts. This breaks composability and may cause funds to be locked if external contracts rely on the interface contract.
